Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded by $y={x}^{2}+3x-2$ and $y=x+1,$ shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the intersection points between the two graphs occur when $x=-3$ and $x=1.$ So these will be our limits of integration.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/299608a54c0b5f568f32619722dd678af1388065f017620071ffb0473a686fa3.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}+3x-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=x+1.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}[\,(x+1)-({x}^{2}+3x-2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1}(-{x}^{2}-2x+3)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded between $y={x}^{2}+2x-9$ and $y=2x+7?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw the graphs of the two functions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/2514c3e7bf5352dbe26dddc479f66042b3736b93f82b97a60850f768a89a4e17.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-9 & =2x+7 \\ {x}^{2} & =16 \\ x & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-4$ to $x=4.$
To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/560fb0937828d5afb5de9593280a1177773598c5d3534ee26318e0bc2788f5ab.png)

 

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}+2x-9,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2x+7.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}[\,(2x+7)-({x}^{2}+2x-9)\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}(-{x}^{2}+16)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}(16-{x}^{2})\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded between $y={x}^{2}-5$ and $y=4x?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/b25bee7ef7257a5611d708eb65b3c8b453b230ad6d2e9289f6cb40dffba89277.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & ={x}^{2}-5 \\ {x}^{2}-4x-5 & =0 \\ (x+1)(x-5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-1$ to $x=5.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/bf79cec9c1ede4a95b3e20415fbf37224ca8616426e8530043fa4a4b54780bab.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}-5,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=4x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{5}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{5}[\,(4x)-({x}^{2}-5)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{5}(-{x}^{2}+4x+5)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{5}(5+4x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded by $y=f(x)=2{x}^{2}-3x+2$ and $y=g(x)=3x-2$, shown above?

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3x+2 & =3x-2 \\ 2{x}^{2}-6x+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-3x+2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=1$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/7d96f51f01c2e52756fe53a6b3a11dd5c7c6dd9cb15ce674a706b442a3e6ad2b.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $f(x)=2{x}^{2}-3x+2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $g(x)=3x-2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[\,(3x-2)-(2{x}^{2}-3x+2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(-2{x}^{2}+6x-4)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded by $y=4{x}^{2}-x$ and $y=2-{x}^{2}-4x?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/913ec93445f3ed571fcf98ad762eba2a1bc657dce7442c8e48fc4d5f36817def.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-x & =2-{x}^{2}-4x \\ 5{x}^{2}+3x-2 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{-3\pm \sqrt{{3}^{2}-4\cdot 5\cdot (-2)}}{2\cdot 5} \\  & =\frac{-3\pm 7}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-1$ to $x=\frac{2}{5}.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/77493917a13269c78acef8ff6fe57b5f350020542805e316f82f7a17dabedd24.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=4{x}^{2}-x,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2-{x}^{2}-4x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{2/5}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2/5}[\,(2-{x}^{2}-4x)-(4{x}^{2}-x)\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2/5}(-5{x}^{2}-3x+2)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-5x & =6-2{x}^{2}-4x \\ 5{x}^{2}-x-6 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{(-1)^{2}-4\cdot 5\cdot (-6)}}{2\cdot 5} \\  & =\frac{1\pm 11}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-1$ to $x=\frac{6}{5}.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/a8c538d5f40f68506588695aa04b38f095360b6f51369d8169099806a9678de9.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=3{x}^{2}-5x,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=6-2{x}^{2}-4x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{6/5}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{6/5}[\,(6-2{x}^{2}-4x)-(3{x}^{2}-5x)\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{6/5}(-5{x}^{2}+x+6)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-5 & =11 \\ {x}^{2} & =16 \\ x & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-4$ to $x=4.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/caf1c4d5df49aa18ed85158615be19745abb7c078269dde35f4e57d57fae292a.png)

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}-5,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=11.$

Therefore, we can find the area as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}[\,(11)-({x}^{2}-5)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}(16-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(16x-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{-4}^{4} \\  & =[16\cdot 4-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {4}^{3}]-[16\cdot (-4)-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-4)^{3}] \\  & =(64-\frac{64}{3})-(-64+\frac{64}{3}) \\  & =\frac{256}{3}.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x & =x \\ {x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ x(x+3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-3$ to $x=0.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/6b2232d5a2853b22c731c317b365822e371f3d419bfcb3e528a07f211a372553.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}+4x,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}[\,(x)-({x}^{2}+4x)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}(-{x}^{2}-3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{-3}^{0} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {0}^{3}-\frac{3}{2}\cdot {0}^{2}]-[-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-3)^{3}-\frac{3}{2}\cdot (-3)^{2}] \\  & =(0)-(9-\frac{27}{2}) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Find the area of the finite region enclosed between $y=4{x}^{2}-1$ and $y=3{x}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/4e3758ddf652c3dd7df10d381b42ca1dde50d48250bed672b740329191202597.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/54ad3b4c8bc3aef707af764cd8d8badf9390737dc75491aa66ea554f531a7576.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=4{x}^{2}-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=3{x}^{2}.$

We can now set up the integration with our $x$ values (Top-Bottom):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(3{x}^{2})-(4{x}^{2}-1)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the integrand is an even function. Therefore, we can find the area, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{(x-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2((1-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {1}^{3})-0) \\  & =2(1-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/5ba7f7b4022c35c4afe7d285c57f87d6fcebfbcd8373ddc530f849e29fbc22de.png)

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6 & =10 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-2$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/3ff79baa7d3d934dd9815b398cbd9f56990011370408ddede51e3c4110b4978c.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}+6,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=10.$

Therefore, we can find the area as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(10)-({x}^{2}+6)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(4x-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =[4\cdot 2-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{3}]-[4\cdot (-2)-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-2)^{3}] \\  & =(8-\frac{8}{3})-(-8+\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Write down an integral that gives the area of the finite region bounded by the curves $y=x^2$ and $y=\sqrt x,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/b98474e6de2c94876a75758d56a7fb356de22bccd029bfeed0207affebab09ce.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the intersection points between the two graphs occur when $x=0$ and $x=1.$ So these will be our limits of integration.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/1b1c2b1826fa988ba23f7270b4c8bbdc91bf03066e8ca3638def329466d5b93e.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=x^2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=\sqrt x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\sqrt{x})-({x}^{2})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{x}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: What is the integral that gives the area of the finite region bounded by $y=x^2+x+5$ and $y=x+9?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/5f6980e3a7e4c7d1a5cc5d9b93a0110764b34ea6b7a4bec7c828f04cef842f7f.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x+5 & =x+9 \\ {x}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-2$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/3c52f1405079380459e60ad35e05218d1f0468ee177f1e383498c672d48eaa8d.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=x^2+x+5,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=x+9.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(x+9)-({x}^{2}+x+5)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area of the finite region enclosed between $f(x) =x^2-2x+2$ and $g(x) = 2,$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/01f139c53b6328341b463f5ad941d37fccb241fff109c0584207017341e8e5f7.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+2 & =2 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013841/assets/39798ef4ff6e898527864628dc2750f88b115c03b2d6b8fb729f30b21d2d2bf5.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=x^2-2x+2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2.$

Therefore, we can find the area as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(2)-({x}^{2}-2x+2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =({2}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{3})-(0-0) \\  & =(4-\frac{8}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
